title: Never Delete an Old Rule Before Passing Chesterton's Fence
alt_title_1: G. K. Chesterton's 1929 Mental Model for Systems & Money
alt_title_2: Why Tearing Down 'Boring' Guardrails Triggers Forgotten Crises
description_hook: In his 1929 book 'The Thing', writer G. K. Chesterton formulated a timeless systems rule: never tear down an old fence until you understand why someone built it. Here is how Chesterton's Fence protects budgets, codebases, and careers.

scenes.headline: The Rookie Impulse to Rip Out Old Rules
scenes.stat_label: WHY BORING GUARDRAILS EXIST FOR A REASON
bullets: Newcomers love deleting checklists, cash buffers, and reviews
Weeks later, a forgotten failure mode comes roaring back
scenes.narration: Every ambitious newcomer wants to tear down clunky old checklists, boring budget buffers, and legacy rules on day one.
scenes.source: G. K. Chesterton, The Thing, Ch. 4 'The Drift from Domesticity' (1929)

scenes.headline: G. K. Chesterton's 1929 Fence Parable
scenes.stat_label: STATE THE ORIGINAL PURPOSE BEFORE DELETING
bullets: Fences do not grow out of country roads by accident
Only reformers who know a rule's origin can safely revise it
scenes.narration: In his 1929 book The Thing, writer G. K. Chesterton imagined a fence blocking a country road. Never tear down a fence, he warned, until you can state the exact reason someone paid to build it.

scenes.headline: Working Guardrails Always Look Unnecessary
scenes.left_body: Cuts emergency cash or QA checks -> revives the original crash
scenes.right_body: Traces historical scar tissue -> upgrades without blind risk
scenes.narration: Effective guardrails look pointless precisely because they work quietly. Deleting emergency cash reserves or pre-launch checks revives the forgotten disaster that originally created them.

scenes.headline: Pass the One-Sentence Origin Audit First
scenes.stat_subtext: Name the original risk + confirm it vanished -> simplify safely
scenes.narration: Apply Chesterton's Audit before cutting any system: trace the failure that birthed the rule, then verify whether that underlying risk actually disappeared.

scenes.headline: Understand First, Simplify Second
bullets: Write one clear sentence explaining what a buffer prevents
Remove obsolete friction only after proving the hazard is gone
scenes.narration: Earn the right to simplify an old guardrail by proving in writing that you understand what it quietly protects.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule of thumb inspired by Chesterton (1929)
